title: What if you tested your own parachute off the Eiffel Tower?

backgrounds.tower: view from the first platform of the Eiffel Tower in 1912, riveted iron railing and wooden deck in the foreground, Paris rooftops and the Seine far below, misty winter morning
backgrounds.airfield: 1911 French airfield, a crashed wooden biplane nose-down in the grass, smoke, a crowd of spectators in hats behind a rope, open grass in the foreground
backgrounds.courtyard: narrow Paris courtyard in 1911 seen from the ground, five storey apartment building with open windows, a broken tailor's dummy lying on the cobbles in the foreground
backgrounds.street: Paris street in 1912 at the foot of the Eiffel Tower, cobblestones, gas lamps, Belle Epoque buildings, cold morning, open pavement in the foreground

lines.text: What if you tested your parachute by jumping off the Eiffel Tower?
Pilots keep dying. There's a prize for a parachute that saves them. You sew one.
Every dummy you throw drops like a rock.
You said you'd use a dummy!
lines.speaker: cop

lines.text: Cameras roll. You wait forty seconds, jump, and it never opens.
Months later, a Russian actor's backpack parachute stops a speeding car dead.
You died. Comment what stupid shenanigans Gary should try tomorrow.

experiment.style: storybook #3 (rewrite of 010 with a real arc, to separate script quality from style)
experiment.arc: goal (prize) -> failed tests -> joke (I am the dummy) -> death -> turn (Kotelnikov's backpack parachute works)
experiment.length: ~30 s (81 words; old scripts ran ~2.6 words/s)
facts: Franz Reichelt, Austrian-born Paris tailor, jumped from the Eiffel Tower's first platform (57 m) on 4 Feb 1912 at about 8:22 and died; he hesitated about 40 s; filmed by Pathe/Gaumont (Wikipedia: Franz Reichelt, contemporary Le Petit Journal / Le Temps reports)
Prizes were offered for an aviator's safety parachute (Colonel Lalance's 10,000 francs via the Aero-Club de France), after a run of fatal flying accidents
Dummy tests from his building's fifth floor failed; he blamed the low height
He got police permission for a dummy test, then jumped himself

Gleb Kotelnikov, a Russian actor, invented the knapsack parachute after seeing a pilot killed in 1910; in June 1912 he proved it by opening it behind a speeding car, which it pulled to a stop (Wikipedia: Gleb Kotelnikov)
